paragraphs.text: For centuries, the ability of bats to fly through complete darkness without striking obstacles was one of the great puzzles of natural history. In the eighteenth century an Italian scientist showed that blinded bats could still avoid threads stretched across a room, while bats whose ears had been blocked collided with them repeatedly. He concluded that bats somehow used their ears to see, but the idea was widely ridiculed, since no one could imagine how hearing might replace vision, and the sounds the bats must be using were beyond the range of human ears. The explanation had to wait for instruments that could detect them.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: In the late 1930s, researchers using a newly developed detector for high-frequency sound finally heard what the bats were doing. The animals were producing rapid calls pitched far above the limit of human hearing and listening for the echoes that returned from objects around them. The term echolocation was coined to describe this, and within a few years it had become clear that the same principle was being developed independently by engineers for detecting submarines and aircraft. The bats, it turned out, had been using a form of sonar for tens of millions of years. Some species are loud enough that, if humans could hear them, their calls would be as noisy as a smoke alarm held close to the ear.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The basic principle is simple, but the detail is remarkable. A bat judges distance from the delay between a call and its echo, direction from the slight differences in timing and loudness between its two ears, and the size and texture of an object from the way the echo is altered. As a bat closes in on an insect, it calls faster and faster, rising from around ten calls a second while searching to as many as two hundred in the final moments of an attack, a rapid burst that researchers call the feeding buzz. A bat can detect a wire thinner than a human hair and distinguish objects that differ in size by only a few millimetres.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Calling so loudly creates an obvious problem: the bat risks deafening itself. Many species solve this by briefly contracting a small muscle in the middle ear just before each call, reducing their sensitivity while they shout and restoring it in time to hear the echo. Others separate the call and the echo by frequency rather than time, producing a long call at a constant pitch and relying on the fact that the echo from a moving object returns at a slightly different pitch, a shift they can detect with extraordinary precision. The mechanism works so quickly that the muscle can relax and contract dozens of times a second.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Bat calls vary greatly between species, and the variation reflects how each hunts. Species that catch insects in open air tend to use loud, low-pitched calls that travel far, while those that pick insects off leaves in dense vegetation use quieter, higher calls that give finer detail over short distances. Some bats that feed on fruit or nectar use echolocation little or not at all and rely mainly on sight and smell, which is a reminder that the familiar image of the bat does not fit every species. A single forest may hold a dozen species, each hunting in its own way and calling at its own characteristic frequencies.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Insects have not been passive victims. Many moths can hear bat calls and respond by diving, looping or dropping to the ground when a bat approaches. Some produce clicking sounds of their own, which appear in certain species to warn bats that they taste unpleasant and in others to interfere with the processing of echoes by the bat. A few moths have wing scales that absorb sound, reducing the strength of the echo they return, an adaptation that researchers have compared to the materials used to make aircraft difficult to detect. Some bats have responded in turn by calling at frequencies that moths hear poorly, or by calling more quietly as they approach.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The study of bats has had practical consequences. Engineers have examined how bats separate their own echoes from those of hundreds of neighbours flying in the same cave, a problem that resembles the interference between devices sharing a radio channel. Researchers have also developed walking aids for people with visual impairments that emit sound and translate the echoes into vibrations or tones, and some blind people have taught themselves to navigate by making clicking sounds with the tongue and listening to how they return, a skill that brain imaging suggests draws on areas normally used for vision. Engineers designing sonar for underwater vehicles have also borrowed ideas from the way bats vary their calls.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Bats themselves face growing pressures. Many species have declined as a result of habitat loss, the removal of old trees and buildings in which they roost, and in some regions disease and collisions with wind turbines. Because echolocating bats can be identified by their calls, recording devices left out overnight now allow researchers to survey populations without catching a single animal. The sounds that were once impossible to hear have become one of the main tools for protecting the animals that make them. Such surveys have already revealed species in places where they had never been recorded.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: The machine that fixed the keyboard

paragraphs.text: Almost everyone who types today uses a keyboard layout designed for a machine that most of them have never touched. The arrangement of letters that begins QWERTY along the top row was settled in the 1870s for mechanical typewriters, and it has survived the arrival of electric machines, computers and touchscreens with remarkably little change. Its persistence is often cited as a classic example of a standard that remains in place not because it is the best available but because too many people and products already depend on it. The layout is now found on devices its designers could never have imagined, from mobile phones to the screens of ticket machines.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Attempts to build a writing machine date back at least to the early eighteenth century, when an English patent was granted for an artificial method of impressing letters, although no description of the device survives. Throughout the following century inventors in several countries produced machines that worked in principle but were slower than handwriting, expensive to make or too delicate for regular use. Many were intended for blind people, for whom a machine that produced legible letters without the need to see the page was of obvious value. Most of these machines survive only as drawings or descriptions, and few were produced in more than a handful of copies.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The machine that reached commercial production in the 1870s was the work of an American newspaper publisher and a group of collaborators, who spent several years refining it before selling the rights to a firearms manufacturer with the capacity to produce it in quantity. In this design each key was connected to a metal bar carrying a letter, and the bars were arranged in a circle beneath the paper. When a key was pressed, its bar swung up and struck an inked ribbon against the page, then fell back to allow the next letter to be typed. The first models printed only capital letters, and the typist could not see what had been typed until the paper was moved forward.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The arrangement of the bars created a problem. If two keys whose bars sat next to each other were pressed in quick succession, the second bar could rise before the first had fallen back, and the two would jam together. The popular explanation of the QWERTY layout is that it was designed to slow typists down to prevent this. Historians who have examined the correspondence of the inventors argue that the aim was rather to separate letters that frequently appear together in English, so that their bars would not be neighbours, which reduced jamming without necessarily slowing anyone down. Jamming was not merely inconvenient, since freeing the bars by hand could smudge the page and slow the typist far more than any layout.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Other explanations have also been proposed. Some researchers point out that the early layout was shaped partly by the needs of telegraph operators, who were among the first professional users of typewriters and needed to transcribe coded messages quickly. The fact that the letters of the word typewriter can all be found on the top row has sometimes been presented as a deliberate feature, allowing salesmen to impress customers by typing the name quickly, although there is no direct evidence that this was intended. Early versions of the layout differed slightly from the modern one, and several letters moved position before the design was fixed.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Once the layout became established, its advantage grew with every machine sold. Typing schools taught it, employers expected it and typists who had learned it had no reason to learn another. Alternative layouts were designed in the twentieth century, the best known of which placed the most frequently used letters on the middle row, where the fingers rest. Its supporters claimed large gains in speed and comfort, but later studies found the advantages to be much smaller than claimed, and the cost of retraining millions of typists was never likely to be accepted. Speed contests between typists using different layouts were held, but they were often organised by supporters of one side.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The influence of the typewriter reached well beyond its keyboard. It opened office work to women on a large scale in the late nineteenth century, since typing was a new skill without an established male workforce, and within a few decades most typists in many countries were women. It also changed the appearance of business correspondence, encouraging standard formats, carbon copies and filing systems that shaped office practice for a century. Many of the office routines it introduced survived long after the machines themselves were replaced.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The mechanical typewriter has almost disappeared, but its layout shows no sign of following it. Computers could easily offer any arrangement of keys, and many allow users to switch layouts with a single setting, yet very few do. The keyboard remains a reminder that the design of a technology can outlive the reasons for it by a very long time, and that once enough people have invested their time in learning something, a better alternative is not always enough to replace it. The same pattern can be seen in other technologies, from the width of railway tracks to the design of electrical plugs.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: In many countries, paying a restaurant bill involves a small decision that has nothing to do with food: how much extra to leave for the people who served it. In some places the tip is a modest gesture, in others a large part of the income of a worker, and in others still it is almost unknown. The practice has been criticised for decades, and in recent years a number of restaurants have abolished it, raising prices instead. The results have been mixed enough to keep the argument alive, and the question of whether tipping should end turns out to be more complicated than either side usually admits. Few everyday customs generate so much disagreement among people who otherwise agree about most things.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The economic argument for tipping is that it rewards good service. Marta Kowalski, an economist who has studied the practice, points out that the evidence for this is surprisingly weak. In studies comparing the size of tips with the ratings customers themselves gave the service, the relationship is positive but small; the amount left depends far more on the size of the bill, the weather, the mood of the customer and whether the server introduced themselves by name. In her view, tipping functions less as a reward for quality than as a social custom that customers follow to avoid embarrassment. Customers who are served by someone they expect to see again, such as in a restaurant they visit regularly, tend to tip more generously.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: James Okoro, who owns several restaurants and abolished tipping in two of them, describes a more practical set of problems. Tips go mainly to the staff who serve customers directly, while cooks and dishwashers, whose work affects the meal just as much, receive little or nothing, and the gap in pay between the front and the back of a restaurant can become a source of resentment. When he replaced tipping with higher prices and a fixed service charge shared among all staff, the kitchen was easier to staff, but some of his most experienced servers left for restaurants where they could earn more from tips. He also found that the atmosphere among staff improved once earnings no longer depended on which tables each server was given.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The reactions of customers have been a further difficulty. Menus without tipping show higher prices, and diners comparing restaurants tend to notice the price on the menu rather than the total they will eventually pay. Several restaurants that abolished tipping have reintroduced it after losing customers to competitors whose menus appeared cheaper. Okoro argues that the change works only if many restaurants in the same area make it together, since a single restaurant that raises its prices is at a disadvantage however honest its pricing. Some restaurants have tried to solve the problem by printing both prices, with and without service, on the menu.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Yuki Tanaka, a sociologist, draws attention to the social meaning of the tip. In countries where tipping is not expected, leaving money can be interpreted as an insult, implying that the worker needs charity or that the service was a personal favour rather than a professional duty. Where tipping is established, on the other hand, it gives customers a sense of control and allows them to express gratitude in a concrete way. She warns that debates conducted in purely economic terms tend to overlook how strongly people feel about these meanings. In some countries, tips are offered discreetly in an envelope, which reflects how carefully the gesture is managed.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The fairness of tipping is questioned most sharply by those who study pay. Elena Ruiz, who researches low-wage work, notes that tips vary with factors that have nothing to do with effort, including the appearance, age and accent of the worker, and that studies in several countries have found consistent differences between groups doing the same job. She also points out that in places where the law allows employers to pay a lower minimum wage to workers who receive tips, the tip effectively subsidises the employer rather than rewarding the employee. Tips paid by card may also take longer to reach workers than cash, and in some businesses part of them has been kept by employers.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Defenders of tipping respond that removing it would simply lower the incomes of many workers. Experienced servers in busy restaurants can earn considerably more from tips than they would from any realistic fixed wage, and many say they prefer a system in which effort and skill can, at least sometimes, be rewarded directly. Kowalski accepts that this is true for some workers but argues that it is not a reason to keep a system whose costs fall mainly on those who earn least.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The most reasonable conclusion is that tipping is neither a pure reward for service nor simply a form of unfairness, but a custom whose effects depend heavily on the laws and expectations surrounding it. Where workers are paid a decent wage regardless of tips, the practice does relatively little harm; where tips are expected to make up for low pay, its weaknesses become serious. Changing it successfully appears to require changes to law and to shared expectations, not simply decisions by individual restaurants.
paragraphs.label: H
